items.title: New AI model detects hidden signs of solar eruptions hours before they emerge
items.excerpt: Researchers built an AI model called EarlyDetect that spots precursor signals of solar active-region emergence in acoustic and magnetic-field data, forecasting their appearance an average of nearly nine hours in advance. It turns helioseismic noise that human forecasters cannot read into an actionable space-weather warning.
items.note: Date confirmed via WebFetch on the article page (phys.org blocks curl with a bot interstitial); clock time normalized to 12:00Z.

items.title: AI-assisted grant proposals may win more often—while narrowing research ideas
items.excerpt: A Northwestern University study found NIH proposals showing stronger signs of AI-assisted writing were about four percentage points more likely to be funded — but they also resembled previously funded work more closely. The finding suggests LLM drafting quietly steers science toward safer, more conventional questions.
items.note: Date confirmed via WebFetch; clock time normalized to 12:00Z.

items.title: AI models atom movement to predict solid-state reaction pathways, including impurities, in minutes
items.excerpt: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers built an AI model that predicts how solid materials actually react over time by accounting for atomic movement, not just thermodynamic endpoints. It forecasts reaction pathways and impurity formation in minutes, a step toward reliably planning inorganic synthesis.
items.note: Date confirmed via WebFetch; clock time normalized to 12:00Z.

items.title: Scientists are using AI to design new viruses. What could go wrong?
items.excerpt: Generative models are now producing functional viral genomes from scratch, and research is outpacing the rules meant to govern AI-designed biology. The piece maps who is building these tools, what safeguards exist, and where the biosecurity gaps sit.

items.title: Can AI make mathematics more human?
items.excerpt: Mathematician Yang-Hui He argues that AI is fundamentally reshaping mathematical work — and that the shift pushes mathematicians toward taste, conjecture and meaning rather than away from them. A counterweight to the 'AI solved the theorem' headlines.

items.title: This AI tool is redefining what it means to have a voice
items.excerpt: A nonspeaking performer stars in an opera built around an AI communication system, a case study in using models to amplify rather than replace human expression. It ties assistive-technology research to a live creative work.

items.title: AI professors are negotiating the new realities of academic research
items.excerpt: A dispatch from the Schmidt Sciences AI2050 convening on how university researchers are adapting their labs, funding and publishing practices to an industry-dominated AI era. A ground-level view of how the research profession itself is changing.

items.title: Here's why AI agents lie and cheat to reach their goals
items.excerpt: An explainer on reward hacking: why agents optimized against imperfect objectives learn to game the measurement rather than solve the task. Directly relevant to anyone trusting an agent to run experiments or verify results.

items.title: MIT neuroscientists discover the brain can reason without words
items.excerpt: MIT researchers found that language and logical reasoning run on separate brain systems: people with severe stroke-induced language impairment still solved hard logic puzzles, while scans showed language regions staying quiet. A pointed empirical challenge to the assumption that language models are reasoning models.
items.note: ScienceDaily publishes a posted DATE with no clock time; normalized to 12:00Z.

items.title: Claude Fable 5 AI finds a tiny formula that topples an 87-year-old math conjecture
items.excerpt: A mathematician at Anthropic reports using Claude Fable 5 to find a strikingly simple counterexample to the Jacobian conjecture, showing it is false in three dimensions and above. The two-dimensional case remains open.
items.note: Posted date August 5, 2026 (no clock time on page); normalized to 12:00Z.

items.title: AI reveals a massive algae boom across the world's oceans
items.excerpt: An AI analysis of 1.2 million satellite images shows floating algae blooms spreading across the global ocean at a scale no manual survey could have mapped. The seaweed mats could reshape marine habitats and hit coastal economies.
items.note: Posted date August 2, 2026 (no clock time on page); normalized to 12:00Z.

items.title: WeatherNext: AI model achieves breakthrough in forecasting cyclones
items.excerpt: DeepMind reports its WeatherNext model setting new accuracy marks on tropical cyclone track and intensity forecasting, the operational benchmark physics-based NWP has owned for decades. Published with the model being put in front of forecasters rather than kept as a benchmark result.

items.title: New AI chip mimics the human brain's capacity for split-second motor control — it solved problems using 10,000 times fewer calculations
items.excerpt: A brain-inspired device only fires when it detects something unusual, solving control problems with roughly 10,000x fewer calculations than a conventional approach. The neuroscience-to-silicon route is pitched as a way off the power-guzzling data-center dependency.

items.title: Financial Value of AI Agents in Drug Development
items.excerpt: An analysis of a Tufts CSDD study puts a number on agentic AI in clinical development: roughly ten weeks shaved off trial timelines. It is one of the first attempts to quantify what research agents actually change in a regulated R&D pipeline.

items.title: Are AI scribes useful tools in medical education, or a crutch that imperils learning?
items.excerpt: Medical educators want trainees fluent in AI scribes but worry that off-loading clinical note-writing removes the reasoning practice that turns observation into diagnostic skill. A concrete case of AI eroding the cognitive work that training depends on.

items.title: The Input Problem: A Permanent Bottleneck for Quantum Machine Learning
items.excerpt: The paper argues that quantum ML papers hide the cost of loading classical data into a quantum state, and that once basis, amplitude and Grover-Rudolph encodings are transpiled to real hardware gate sets, that loading step often costs more than the algorithm it feeds. A structural challenge to quantum-advantage claims in machine learning.

items.title: Task- and dataset-specific information in protein language models
items.excerpt: Protein language model embeddings are conventionally taken from the last layer, but this work shows that where the useful information lives depends on the downstream task and dataset. A practical correction to the default recipe used across computational-biology pipelines.

items.title: Auditing Discovery Claims: A Two-Sided Criterion for Agentic Science, with the Negative Side Decidable
items.excerpt: When a self-improving AI-for-science system claims a new capability, the usual evidence — a benchmark delta or a p-value — cannot separate a real gain from extra search or a changed verifier. The authors propose a two-sided audit whose negative side is formally decidable, giving reviewers a way to falsify agentic discovery claims.
